newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal, India to enforce water sharing treaty.
newsitem.headline: Nepal, India to enforce water sharing treaty.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral will arrive in the Nepali capital on Thursday to formalise a water sharing treaty boosting economic cooperation with the Himalayan kingdom, officials said.

Gujral and his Nepali counterpart Lokendra Bahadur Chand will exchange instruments of ratification putting into force the treaty for the development of the Mahakali river in west Nepal, Nepali Foreign Secretary Kumar Gyawali said.
The treaty, signed in 1996, was ratified by Nepal's split parliament in September last year after intense political jockeying.

It covers the construction of a dam on the Mahakali river on the kingdom's western borders with India to generate up to 6,400 megawatts (mw) of hydroelectric power to be equally shared by the two countries.

Nepal will export its share of excess electricity to power-starved areas of India whose present shortage of electricity is estimated at 12,000 mw, and help bridge its large trade deficit of $308 million with New Delhi.
Officials said the two countries will sign a power trade agreement allowing private firms to produce hydropower in Nepal for export to India.
"It is a very innovative agreement because it is an enabling document to attract private investment and trade in the power sector," India's ambassador to Nepal K.V. Rajan told Reuters.
Nepal welcomes private funds to tap its potential of about 83,000 mw of hydroelectric power and sell in India, which allows almost all Nepali products duty free entry into its market.
There are over 100 joint venture projects with India worth $304 million, or 40 percent of all foreign investment in Nepal, an Indian official said.
Officials said Gujral will meet King Birendra, the world's only Hindu monarch, and hold discussions with Prime Minister Chand and other Nepali leaders.

Gujral is scheduled to lay the foundation stone of a 200-bed Emergency and Trauma Centre at a hospital in Kathmandu which would be South Asia's first such facility providing high quality emergency services.
Land-locked Nepal also wants permission to use a 71 km (44 mile) route across India to give its traders easy access to the Bangladesh port of Chittagong.
India provides other routes at present but Nepal says that this route would be more viable. At present, Nepali traders use Calcutta port for their cargo which at times gets very congested.
The Bangladesh government has already allowed Nepal to use Chittagong and India has agreed in principle to grant the access. Officials of Nepal and India are at present discussing the details.
